questions.question: Examine the common properties and trends of metals, non-metals, and metalloids in the periodic table.
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the common properties and trends of metals, non-metals and metalloids in the
  • periodic table.
  • Metals include the alkali metal, alkaline earth, transition metal, lanthanide and actinide groups.
  •  At room temperature, they are usually solids (except mercury).
  •  They usually have high boiling and melting points.
  •  They are shiny having a metallic luster.
  •  They are good conductors of heat and electricity.
  • Non-metals exhibit a variety of physical and chemical properties that are distinct from those of
  • metals. Nonmetals display the following properties
  •  They are brittle and are not malleable or ductile.
  •  At room temperature, they are usually solids or gases.
  •  They usually have low boiling and melting points (except for carbon and boron).
  •  They are poor conductors of heat and electricity.
  • Metalloids exhibit some properties of metals as well as non- metals. Hence, they are also known
  • as semi-metals. Boron, Silicon, Germanium, Arsenic, Antimony, and Tellurium are the most
  • commonly recognized metalloids.
  •  They may have a metallic or dull appearance.
  •  They are usually brittle and fair conductors of electricity.
  •  They may gain or lose electrons during chemical reactions.
  •  They form alloys with metals.
  • (Give full credit if any three relevant properties of each is given with examples)

questions.question: What are quantum numbers? Discuss the significance of quantum numbers.
questions.solution_html:
•  Definition of quantum numbers
  •  Types and significance (Principal quantum number (n), Subsidiary or azimuthal
  • quantum number (l), Magnetic quantum number (m), Spin quantum number (s))
  •  The principal quantum number (n) determines the energy level and size of an orbital
  • while the azimuthal quantum number (l) defines its shape. The magnetic quantum
  • number (m) specifies the orientation of the orbital in space, and the spin quantum
  • number (s) indicates the direction of the electron's intrinsic spin, either +½ or -½.
  •  Values of quantum numbers
  • 'n' can have values, 1, 2, 3, 4 etc
  • '1' and can have values from 0 to n – 1
  • The values of m are -'l' through zero to + 'l' and thus there are (2l + 1) values possible
  • spin quantum number can have only values +1/2 or -1/2.
  • (Definition- (2 marks), Significance - (5 marks))

questions.question: Explain the limitations of Bohr theory.
questions.solution_html:
• Bohr theory's limitations include its inability to explain the spectra of atoms with
  • more than one electron, its failure to account for the Zeeman and Stark effects
  • (the splitting of spectral lines in magnetic and electric fields, respectively), and its
  • contradiction of the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle. The theory also could not
  • explain the fine structure of spectral lines, the relative intensities of those lines, or
  • why atoms form chemical bonds to create molecules. (any 5 points full mark)
questions.final_answer: why atoms form chemical bonds to create molecules. (any 5 points full mark)

questions.question: How does hyperconjugation differ from the inductive effect in stabilizing / carbocations? Provide examples to explain their roles.
questions.solution_html:
• carbocations? Provide examples to explain their roles.
  • Hyperconjugation is the delocalization of sigma electrons from adjacent C-H
  • bonds into an empty p-orbital of a carbocation, while the inductive effect is the
  • transmission of charge through sigma bonds due to differences in
  • electronegativity. Hyperconjugation involves the overlap of a sigma bond with a p
  • orbital, which distributes the positive charge, and is a more effective stabilizing
  • mechanism for carbocations than the inductive effect, which involves a purely
  • polar effect.
  • Example: Tertiary Butyl Carbocation ((CH₃)₃C⁺)
  • The central carbon is attached to three methyl groups. Each methyl group has
  • three C–H bonds, adjacent to the positively charged carbon.
  • These σ C–H bonds overlap with the empty p-orbital of the carbocation. This
  • allows hyperconjugation up to 9 structures can contribute. This delocalization
  • reduces the positive charge density on the carbocation, making it much more
  • stable. (difference (4 marks), example (3 marks))
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025

questions.question: Explain the delocalization of electrons, the concept of contributing / resonance structures, and the impact of resonance on the stability of a molecule.
questions.solution_html:
• resonance structures, and the impact of resonance on the stability of a
  • molecule.
  • Delocalization refers to the spreading of electrons rather than being confined between
  • two atoms. This occurs in systems with conjugated double bonds or lone pairs
  • adjacent to π bonds. Example: In benzene (C₆H₆), the six π electrons are not
  • localized between specific carbon atoms but are delocalized across the entire ring.
  • This leads to equal bond lengths between all carbon atoms.
  • Contributing resonance structures are multiple valid Lewis structures that represent
  • different possible electron arrangements within the same molecule. Resonance
  • stabilization lowers the overall energy of a molecule. It distributes charges and
  • electron density more evenly. Molecules with resonance are typically less reactive
  • and more stable than those without. (explanation (2 marks), contributing structure 3
  • marks, stability (2 marks))

questions.question: Explain the reasons behind the anomalous properties of elements like / nitrogen, fluorine and oxygen within their respective groups.
questions.solution_html:
• nitrogen, fluorine and oxygen within their respective groups.
  • Small Atomic Size: very small atomic radii, leading to a large charge-to-radius
  • ratio. This affects properties like ionization enthalpy and electronegativity.
  • High Electronegativity: highest electronegativity values, is a major factor in the
  • formation of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds in their hydrides, results in high
  • melting and boiling points compared to other group member hydrides.
  • Absence of Vacant d-Orbitals: The valence shells of second-period elements
  • only contain s and p orbitals (2s and 2p). The absence of vacant d-orbitals limits
  • their maximum covalency to four (one s and three p orbitals)
  • Tendency to Form Multiple pπ–pπ Bonds: Due to their small size, the p-orbitals
  • of nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine can overlap effectively side-on to form stable pπ–
  • pπ multiple bonds with themselves and other small elements like carbon. This
  • results in the existence of stable diatomic molecules.
  • (full mark for reasonable attempt)
questions.final_answer: Option (d) Orbitals: The valence shells of second-period elements

questions.question: How does hyperconjugation differ from the inductive effect in stabilizing / carbocations? Provide examples to explain their roles.
questions.solution_html:
• carbocations? Provide examples to explain their roles.
  • Hyperconjugation is the delocalization of sigma electrons from adjacent C-H
  • bonds into an empty p-orbital of a carbocation, while the inductive effect is the
  • transmission of charge through sigma bonds due to differences in
  • electronegativity. Hyperconjugation involves the overlap of a sigma bond with a p
  • orbital, which distributes the positive charge, and is a more effective stabilizing
  • mechanism for carbocations than the inductive effect, which involves a purely
  • polar effect.
  • Example: Tertiary Butyl Carbocation ((CH₃)₃C⁺)
  • The central carbon is attached to three methyl groups. Each methyl group has
  • three C–H bonds, adjacent to the positively charged carbon.
  • These σ C–H bonds overlap with the empty p-orbital of the carbocation. This
  • allows hyperconjugation up to 9 structures can contribute. This delocalization
  • reduces the positive charge density on the carbocation, making it much more
  • stable. (difference (4 marks), example (3 marks))

questions.question: Explain the delocalization of electrons, the concept of contributing / resonance structures, and the impact of resonance on the stability of a molecule.
questions.solution_html:
• resonance structures, and the impact of resonance on the stability of a
  • molecule.
  • Delocalization refers to the spreading of electrons rather than being confined between
  • two atoms. This occurs in systems with conjugated double bonds or lone pairs
  • adjacent to π bonds. Example: In benzene (C₆H₆), the six π electrons are not
  • localized between specific carbon atoms but are delocalized across the entire ring.
  • This leads to equal bond lengths between all carbon atoms.
  • Contributing resonance structures are multiple valid Lewis structures that represent
  • different possible electron arrangements within the same molecule. Resonance
  • stabilization lowers the overall energy of a molecule. It distributes charges and
  • electron density more evenly. Molecules with resonance are typically less reactive
  • and more stable than those without. (explanation (2 marks), contributing structure 3
  • marks, stability (2 marks))

  • ratio. This affects properties like ionization enthalpy and electronegativity.
  • High Electronegativity: highest electronegativity values, is a major factor in the
  • formation of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds in their hydrides, results in high

  • only contain s and p orbitals (2s and 2p). The absence of vacant d-orbitals limits
  • their maximum covalency to four (one s and three p orbitals)

  • of nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine can overlap effectively side-on to form stable pπ–
  • pπ multiple bonds with themselves and other small elements like carbon. This
